newsitem.title: JAPAN: Gloom seen continuing for Japan construction firms.
newsitem.headline: Gloom seen continuing for Japan construction firms.

text.p: Japanese construction firms, lurking in the shadow of the nation's massive bad loan problems, have little hope for a strong rise in profits in coming business years, analysts say.
"I don't expect builders' earnings to rise handsomely soon," Hideki Harima, analyst at the Wako Research Institute of Economics, said.
"The top four builders, for example, will clear their 1996/97 forecast and their profit may increase in 1997/98. But I am not sure about the next year," he added.

The four, Shimizu Corp, Kajima Corp, Taisei Corp and Obayashi Corp, have said they would meet their earnings targets for the 1996/97 financial year, which ends March 31. But they have declined to comment on profits after 1997/98.
"The construction and banking industries are the two biggest negative factors in Japan's present economy," one analyst said.
The two sectors were both active participants in Japan's 1980s "bubble" era of skyrocketing asset prices, and were left with heaps of bad loans after the bubble burst in early 1990.

Builders led the bubble-era investment in property and real estate and also guaranteed their real estate units' loans. Banks, meanwhile, aggressively extended loans for real estate projects, often because they were guaranteed by builders.
The amount of debts guaranteed by the 98 Japanese builders totalled 3.22 trillion yen ($26.1 billion) at the end of September 1996, according to leading credit research firm Teikoku Databank Ltd.

The construction industry was further tainted by allegations of bid-rigging by some of the top firms in public works tenders, resulting in the arrests of senior officials and a suspension of some firms from bidding for public projects.

In the latest scandal, the Asahi Shimbun reported earlier this month that Japan's anti-monopoly watchdog Fair Trade Commission has launched an investigation into allegations made by a senior executive of Nishimatsu Construction Co Ltd of bid-rigging in western Japan.

Analysts said the new scandal might become a fresh blow to the construction industry, whose shares have fallen to average 770 yen ($6) in the middle of March, down from about 940 yen ($7) at the beginning of the year.
There is little scope to boost shares in the near future.
Orders from both public and private sectors are not expected to rise sharply as Japan is considering a cut in its public works spending to reduce overall expenditures.
The slow economic recovery is likely to keep manufacturers and other firms from planning large capital spending, they added.
"The gap in the volume of orders may widen between construction firms," said Hiroyuki Chikusa, analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.
Profit margins are recovering, but the rise is only in reaction to the sharp drop in margins caused by severe competition over private sector projects a few years ago.
Analysts said Japan's top four construction firms are currently aiming to write off their bad assets even if it means they will post a net profit just large enough to pay dividends.
But they said some of the smaller builders are shouldering a heavier bad debt burden and are likely to slip into the red.
"They will have to make a decision to post losses at some point when interest rates start rising," another analyst said.
Tobishima Corp, Aoki Corp, Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd, Mitsui Construction Co Ltd and Kumagai Gumi Co Ltd topped Teikoku's list of builders which have guaranteed huge loans which may not be recoverable.
Tobishima and Aoki have said they would post slightly larger parent current profits in 1996/97 but the other three expect profit declines for the year.

While many of the smaller firms are able to absorb the losses themselves, some will be forced to turn to their creditors for support -- banks which themselves are struggling with bad loans and may not have the option to support them.

Tobishima has already asked its creditors to accept its restructuring plan, which includes a reduction in creditors' claims against Tobishima for its group companies' debt to 100 billion yen ($813 million) from about 740 billion yen ($6.01 billion).

Tobishima has said that it believes the plan will be accepted. Its main bank, Fuji Bank Ltd, said that many of the creditors have responded positively to the restructuring though they are yet to decide whether to accept the plan.
